title: India's Supreme Court Just Rebuked Its Own Bench on UAPA Bail — and the Implications Are Enormous
excerpt: In a pointed departure from a January ruling that kept Umar Khalid and Sharjeel Imam behind bars, a new bench has reasserted that 'bail is the rule, jail is the exception' — even under India's harshest anti-terror law
body:
The Supreme Court of India rarely contradicts itself in public. When it does, the legal community pays attention. This week, a bench heard arguments in the bail application of Syed Ifthikar Andrabi — a Kashmiri man charged under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act in a narco-terrorism case — and used the occasion to deliver what amounted to a judicial rebuke of a ruling handed down by a coordinate bench just four months ago.

In January 2026, a different Supreme Court bench had denied bail to Umar Khalid and Sharjeel Imam, both accused in the 2020 Delhi riots conspiracy case under UAPA. That ruling had effectively sidelined the landmark 2021 judgment in K.A. Najeeb v. Union of India, which established that prolonged pre-trial incarceration itself could be grounds for bail, even under stringent statutes like UAPA.

## A Constitutional Correction

The new bench did not merely disagree. It characterised the January ruling as having ignored binding precedent. "The principle that bail is the rule and jail is the exception is not a platitude," the bench observed. "It is a constitutional imperative flowing from Article 21." The court emphasised that K.A. Najeeb, decided by a three-judge bench, remained the controlling authority and could not be whittled down by a two-judge bench.

Andrabi was granted bail. But the significance extends far beyond his case. Legal scholars immediately noted that the court's reasoning effectively reopened the question of whether Khalid and Imam — who have been incarcerated for over six years without trial — might now have stronger grounds for a fresh bail application.

## UAPA: The Law That Swallows Liberty

The Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act is India's most powerful anti-terror statute. Under Section 43D(5), courts are prohibited from granting bail if, on a prima facie reading, the accusation appears true. This reversal of the normal presumption of innocence has made UAPA the government's instrument of choice for cases involving allegations of sedition, terrorism, and organised crime.

Human rights organisations have long argued that UAPA's bail provisions amount to preventive detention by another name. According to data compiled by the National Crime Records Bureau, the conviction rate under UAPA is below 3 per cent, yet the average pre-trial detention exceeds four years. Critics call it a law designed not to convict but to confine.

## The Delhi Riots Shadow

The Delhi riots cases remain the most politically charged UAPA prosecutions in recent memory. Khalid, a former JNU student leader, and Imam, an activist, were arrested in 2020 for allegedly conspiring to incite the communal violence that killed 53 people in northeast Delhi. The prosecution's case relies heavily on WhatsApp messages and speeches, which defence lawyers argue have been taken out of context.

The January denial of bail had prompted protests from civil liberties groups and drew criticism from international human rights bodies. Amnesty International called it "a dark day for judicial independence in India." The government defended the ruling as consistent with the gravity of the charges.

## Why the Diaspora Is Watching

For the Indian diaspora — particularly in the United States, United Kingdom, and Canada, where UAPA cases have featured in parliamentary debates and editorial pages — the Supreme Court's internal tension offers both hope and anxiety. Hope, because the reassertion of bail principles suggests the judiciary has not entirely ceded ground on civil liberties. Anxiety, because the existence of contradictory rulings from the same court creates uncertainty about which precedent will prevail.

The practical test will come when Khalid or Imam files a fresh bail application citing the Andrabi ruling. If a bench grants it, it would mark one of the most significant judicial course corrections in Indian criminal law. If it does not, the contradiction will stand — a monument to the unresolved tension between national security and individual freedom that defines UAPA's place in Indian jurisprudence.

For now, the court has spoken twice and said two different things. The next word will matter most.
